title: The Woman in Cabin 10
synopsis: A luxury cruise. A woman in the next cabin. A splash at two a.m. By morning, the cabin doesn't exist and neither does she. You're a journalist, mid-breakdown, expected to write a glossy travel piece. Try not to.

nodes.text: Eight cabins, eleven passengers, and a press kit that has spelled your surname two different ways on facing pages. The brief is four thousand words on the canapes and the northern lights. Your hands are not steady and it is not the drink. It is the man who was in your flat on Sunday while you lay behind the bedroom door, breathing through your mouth, pretending to be furniture.

choices.consequence: You put on the dress and the voice and work the room. Nine people will later swear you seemed absolutely fine. You commit to network at the welcome dinner. It carries you into Cabin 10 while the safer possibility closes without making a sound.

You take the far end of the bar and watch instead. You will end up the only person aboard who can describe what everybody wore. You stay quiet and observe. The way toward The Owner opens, and something on the other side seems to notice.

nodes.text: You knock next door for mascara and get it, along with a Pink Floyd T-shirt several sizes too big for her and a face that has been assembled in a hurry. Mid-thirties, thin, English but not from anywhere she wants to name. You make a joke about the satellite Wi-Fi. She laughs half a second late and far too hard, and shuts the door before you finish saying thanks.

choices.text: Take note of her name and accent
choices.consequence: You do not get a name. You get the accent, the shirt and a lipstick colour, and one day soon that will be the entire case. You choose to take note of her name and accent. By Two A.M., the danger will know a little more about you than you know about it.

choices.text: Move on; she's just a stranger
choices.consequence: You go back to your cabin and think about your own week instead. Tomorrow you will hate yourself for how ordinary that was. You move on; she's just a stranger. The way toward Cabin 10, Morning opens, and something on the other side seems to notice.

nodes.text: Richard Bullmer works the saloon the way a man does who has been trained on rooms since prep school — a hand at an elbow, a name recalled, a joke that flatters whoever receives it. His wife Anne is the money, everybody knows it, and she says perhaps nine words all evening. She watches him perform with the fixed attention of someone checking a script she wrote herself.

choices.consequence: She gives you four minutes, all of it charming and none of it usable. Her wedding ring turns loose on the finger while she talks. You try to interview Anne. The way toward Two A.M. opens, and something on the other side seems to notice.
He talks for forty minutes about his own boyhood and asks you nothing. You leave with three quotes and the feeling you were the one interviewed.

nodes.text: The sound wakes you before you have language for it. Not a wave, not a deck chair going over — the flat heavy slap of a weight entering cold water from a height. You are on the veranda in six seconds. Next door's balcony door stands open with the curtain breathing out into the wind, and along the top of the rail there is a dark smear the width of a hand.

choices.consequence: You go over the divider barefoot. The cabin is dark, the bed made, the shelf above the sink wiped, the mascara gone. You choose to run to Cabin 10. By The Cleaner, the danger will know a little more about you than you know about it.

You do the correct thing and lose four minutes to a hold tone. Four minutes is plenty if two people are working quickly. You choose to call security from your room. By The Captain, the danger will know a little more about you than you know about it.

nodes.text: You ask after your neighbour over the eggs and the crew are charming and utterly blank. Cabin ten was empty on the outbound leg — nobody assigned, nobody boarded, here is the manifest, would you like more coffee. When you get inside, the room has been cleaned past cleanliness: no water ring, no hair in the drain, the pillows creased in the exact shape the housekeeping manual specifies.

choices.consequence: You start behaving like a guest enjoying herself, which turns out to be the most exhausting work you have ever done. You choose to investigate quietly. By The Cleaner, the danger will know a little more about you than you know about it.

You go up the chain inside the hour. It gets you the truth faster and it tells everyone aboard precisely what you know. You push the captain immediately. The way toward The Captain opens, and something on the other side seems to notice.

nodes.text: Eva is nineteen, from Cebu, on a nine-month contract that four people at home are living on. She drops a tray in front of you and apologises for a full minute, which is fifty seconds longer than the tray deserved. When you say the words cabin ten, her hands stop moving on the cloth. Then she tells you, in very careful English, that she has a great many cabins to do.

choices.consequence: You spend two days learning her rota, her sister's name and what she is owed in back pay. It costs you time you may not have. You commit to win Eva's trust slowly. It carries you into Anne, Glimpsed while the safer possibility closes without making a sound.

choices.text: Press Eva quickly while she's rattled
choices.consequence: You get one sentence out of her before her supervisor rounds the corner. You also get her reassigned to the night shift by lunchtime. You commit to press Eva quickly while she's rattled. It carries you into Your Editor while the safer possibility closes without making a sound.

nodes.text: Larsen is fifty-something, courteous, and exhausted in a way that has nothing to do with sleep. He hears you out without once interrupting, checks a screen he does not need to check, and tells you there is no occupant in cabin ten. Then he thanks you for raising it. Then he holds your eye two beats too long, and what is in his face is not disbelief. It is a warning.

choices.consequence: He says the aft camera has been down since Bergen, which is true, and which he knows sounds exactly like a lie. You push for the security footage. The way toward Anne, Glimpsed opens, and something on the other side seems to notice.

choices.text: Back down to keep his trust
choices.consequence: You apologise for the fuss and let him believe it was nerves. That night he starts leaving doors unlocked that should not be. You back down to keep his trust. The way toward Your Editor opens, and something on the other side seems to notice.

nodes.text: Crew deck, aft, where guests do not go. Anne is thirty feet away with her back to you in the coat from dinner, and everything about her is wrong — shoulders too narrow, weight on the wrong foot, a stride that eats more ground than a woman of that height should manage. Then she turns, and it is Anne's face, unmistakably Anne's face, and you stop trusting your own eyes entirely.

choices.consequence: Four frames on the phone, every one of them grainy and none of them provable. You back them up in three places anyway. You commit to photograph from a distance. It carries you into Richard's Charm while the safer possibility closes without making a sound.

You say her name and watch her decide, in under a second, which of two people to be. She chooses extremely well. You commit to approach her openly. It carries you into Eva's Tip while the safer possibility closes without making a sound.

nodes.text: You send the careful email, the one that avoids the word body and mentions security and process and a possible incident. Rowan replies in nine minutes from a phone in a taxi: Got it. Focus on the canapes, filing Tuesday. Then the satellite link drops for the scheduled maintenance the daily newsletter has been promising all week, and the ship stops being a ship and becomes an island.

choices.text: Schedule a sat-phone call with your friend
choices.consequence: You book eight minutes on the bridge phone for Thursday and write a friend's number in the log. Somebody reads that log. You commit to schedule a sat-phone call with your friend. It carries you into Richard's Charm while the safer possibility closes without making a sound.

choices.text: Keep notes locally in a paper notebook
choices.consequence: You write it all out by hand in the back of the press pack — times, names, the exact word Larsen used. Paper cannot be wiped remotely. You choose to keep notes locally in a paper notebook. By Eva's Tip, the danger will know a little more about you than you know about it.

nodes.text: He offers you the engine room, the wheelhouse, the wine store, all of it, just the two of you. Then he mentions the Corby piece you wrote in 2017 — not the famous one, the one that ran on a bank holiday and got pulled inside a week. He has read it. He has read the follow-up as well. Nobody on this boat is supposed to know your byline that thoroughly.

choices.text: Take the tour, alert and unflattering
choices.consequence: You go, and you make yourself boring: no questions, no notes, wide eyes. Below deck he shows you a door and then talks over it. You choose to take the tour, alert and unflattering. By Storm Night, the danger will know a little more about you than you know about it.

You plead seasickness and stay in a public lounge until midnight. He is gracious about it, and afterwards you are alone in a new way. You refuse politely with a cover. The way toward The Body opens, and something on the other side seems to notice.

nodes.text: A folded note falls out of the fresh towels. The handwriting is tiny and unslanted, the writing of someone taught to write neatly in a second language. She was in the laundry corridor one whole day. I think she got out before I cleaned. Please do not say my name. There is no signature. At the bottom there is a small drawn arrow, pointing down.

choices.text: Check the laundry corridor at night
choices.consequence: You go at quarter past two in a borrowed crew jacket with a mop as a prop. Somebody has been sleeping behind the linen carts. You commit to check the laundry corridor at night. It carries you into Storm Night while the safer possibility closes without making a sound.

choices.text: Try to find any port-of-call sighting
choices.consequence: You cross-reference the shore-excursion sign-out sheets in the library. Two names on the Trondheim list never came back aboard. You choose to try to find any port-of-call sighting. By The Body, the danger will know a little more about you than you know about it.

nodes.text: Force nine off the Lofoten shelf. The ship drops out from under you between one step and the next and glasses walk off tables by themselves. In the crew galley, behind a wall of crates lashed down for weather, a woman in a stolen chef's jacket is braced on the floor with her heels against the bulkhead. She has been eating out of tins for six days. She looks up. You heard it, she says.

choices.text: Hide her in your cabin until port
choices.consequence: Two of you, one bed, forty hours, stewards knocking twice a day. You sleep in shifts so that one of you is always awake. You choose to hide her in your cabin until port. By The Identity, the danger will know a little more about you than you know about it.

choices.text: Help her radio for help externally
choices.consequence: You get her to a handheld radio on the bridge wing at four in the morning. The transmission lasts nine seconds and somebody ashore logs it. You help her radio for help externally. The way toward Port of Tromsø opens, and something on the other side seems to notice.

nodes.text: She comes ashore on the rocks below a fishing village outside Bodo in the second week. The crew are told it was a cleaner who went over the side drunk, and the crew, who are all on nine-month contracts, agree that this is very sad. But no cleaner is missing. Every one of them is accounted for. You understand what you are looking at: a body chosen to be somebody.

choices.consequence: You find a coroner's clerk in Bodo willing to talk off the record about dental work. The dental work is Eastern European. You commit to investigate the body's identity privately. It carries you into The Identity while the safer possibility closes without making a sound.

choices.text: Get to a journalist friend in Oslo
choices.consequence: You call Marit in Oslo, who owes you nothing and comes anyway. Within a day the same questions are being asked in two countries. You choose to get to a journalist friend in Oslo. By Port of Tromsø, the danger will know a little more about you than you know about it.

nodes.text: The woman from cabin ten is a private investigator out of Manchester, hired eight months ago by Anne's brothers to establish where the money was actually going. She came aboard on a forged crew pass. And the elegant woman in the good coat who has been signing documents as Anne Bullmer since Bergen has never been Anne Bullmer. She is paid, she is frightened, and she is the second person aboard being disposed of.

choices.consequence: You start with the private clinics, the ones that take cash and ask about family history rather than next of kin. There are six on that coast.

You go loud. The double runs inside a day, and the man who hired her is left holding a paper trail with nobody at the end of it. You expose the double publicly. The way toward The Piece opens, and something on the other side seems to notice.

nodes.text: You come down the gangway at eight in the morning with her wrapped in your coat and your press card in your fist. The detective who takes the statement is a woman of about fifty who has heard every version of cruise-ship nonsense and who, crucially, believes this one inside twenty minutes. She takes the coat as evidence. She gives you a blanket and a phone. She never once asks whether you had been drinking.

choices.text: Stay in Norway through the investigation
choices.consequence: You take a room above a bakery in Tromso for five weeks. It is dark by two in the afternoon and you sleep, finally, straight through. You stay in Norway through the investigation. The way toward Anne's Cabin opens, and something on the other side seems to notice.

choices.text: Get on a plane to London to make noise
choices.consequence: You are at the desk by Tuesday with your notes and a media lawyer. Rowan reads the first four hundred words standing up, in his coat. You get on a plane to London to make noise. The way toward The Piece opens, and something on the other side seems to notice.

nodes.text: They find her at a private clinic at the head of a fjord, registered under a name that means nothing, on a sedation regimen no doctor there will put a signature to. It takes nine days to bring her back to language and much longer to bring her back to her own history. On the second afternoon her hand comes across the blanket and closes on yours. She says your name. She has read you for years.

choices.text: Stay with her family in the recovery
choices.consequence: You cancel everything and sit in a corridor with her brothers for three weeks. It is not journalism, and it is the right thing. You stay with her family in the recovery. The way toward The Trial opens, and something on the other side seems to notice.
You start the file that night in a hotel room with a chair against the door. Every paragraph gets sourced twice before you allow yourself the next.

nodes.text: Nine thousand words, four countries, three named sources and one who will only ever be a letter of the alphabet. Rowan reads it twice — actually reads it, for the first time in six years — and walks it into legal himself. It runs on a Sunday. By Wednesday two banks have frozen facilities and a charter fleet is impounded in Southampton. Nobody, anywhere, asks you about the canapes.

choices.text: Push for criminal charges in the wake of the piece
choices.consequence: You hand your notes to a prosecutor in Oslo and accept that the story now goes somewhere you have no control over at all. You push for criminal charges in the wake of the piece. The way toward The Trial opens, and something on the other side seems to notice.

You file, switch the phone off, and sleep fourteen hours. The rest of it happens without you, and that is allowed. You choose to take the publication and rest. By Your Editor's Apology, the danger will know a little more about you than you know about it.

nodes.text: Bullmer stands trial in Oslo across nine weeks. Two of his officers turn and one of his lawyers resigns halfway through. Anne testifies on video from a room with soft furniture and stays steady the whole time. And Eva — nineteen, contract expired, flown in and housed by the state — details a year of what the staff saw and were paid not to see, in her third language, without hesitating once.

choices.consequence: You sit through all nine weeks on a bench that wrecks your back. For the last three days you take no notes at all. You commit to stay involved for the verdict. It carries you into The Verdict while the safer possibility closes without making a sound.

choices.text: Decline further coverage; protect your nerves
choices.consequence: You hand the file to Marit and stop reading the wires. Your therapist calls it a boundary. You call it running. Both are true. You choose to decline further coverage; protect your nerves. By Off The Boat, the danger will know a little more about you than you know about it.

nodes.text: Rowan takes you to the Italian place he uses when something is going to be said properly. He apologises for the taxi email, for the word canapes, and for six years of treating the shake in your hands as the most interesting fact about you. Then he offers you a column — weekly, your subject, your call. You let him sit in the silence a while before you say yes.

choices.text: Use the column for investigations like this one
choices.consequence: You tell him you want the ugly ones, and he pretends not to look relieved. The first pitch is already in your bag under the table. You commit to use the column for investigations like this one. It carries you into First Column Pitch while the safer possibility closes without making a sound.

choices.text: Use the column for something you actually love
choices.consequence: You tell him you want ports, kitchens, weather and the people working the night shift. He blinks twice and says fine. You use the column for something you actually love. The way toward First Column Pitch opens, and something on the other side seems to notice.

nodes.text: Friday deadline, Thursday night, two outlines on the desk under the same lamp. One opens with a body on rocks and will sell. The other opens with the smell of a harbour at five in the morning and the men unloading it, and will not. You are not choosing a subject here. You are choosing which of two women goes on the masthead for the next decade.

choices.consequence: You send the one with the bodies in it, and you hear the click of a door opening behind you that will not close again. You commit to pitch the investigative beat. It carries you into The Column while the safer possibility closes without making a sound.

You send the harbours, and half of you calls it cowardice for about a year, and then that half goes quiet. You pitch the travel column, properly. The way toward Travel Writer, Properly opens, and something on the other side seems to notice.

nodes.text: He is convicted on the Monday. Anne keeps the company and converts two of the ships into something that carries doctors instead of billionaires. Eva is paid every krone of her withheld wages and takes a shore job in Bergen on a contract you could read without flinching. You are in the public gallery with a notebook you never open once, and when you hold it up to the light your hands are perfectly steady.

You take six months and learn to sleep in a room with the door shut. Your therapist suggests something with your hands in it, so you take up pottery and are patient, dogged and spectacularly bad at it. Out of an entire term you produce one usable cup — lopsided, glazed the wrong blue, heavy on the left. You drink from it every morning as evidence that you are on dry land and it holds.

The column matters, which you had not entirely expected. Two more cases break out of it in five years and one of them ends a minister. The byline is spelled correctly everywhere now, including in the letters from lawyers. You still check the lock twice. But you are working, and you are good at it, and the woman who could not hold a glass in that press-kit photograph is somebody you visit rather than somebody you are.

You take the column and write about coastlines, about hotel kitchens at four in the morning, about the exact smell of a small port before the ice trucks come. Almost none of it is about murder. Readers write in about places they grew up and get the geography wrong and you print their letters anyway. It takes three years to admit the thing you were dodging on that ship: you were always a very good travel writer.
